sections.heading: Simplified synthesis of C-Z nanostructures
sections.text: Simplified synthesis of C-Z nanostructures The fabrication of C-Z nanostructures is a pioneering and simplified method that does not require surfactants, pH adjustment, centrifugation, or hazardous chemicals. This novel approach demands only two precursor substances: zinc nitrate hexahydrate (Zn(NO 3 ) 2 ·6H 2 O) and the organic compound furfural (C 4 H 3 OCHO). The procedure began by manually blending the precursors in a mortar using a pestle for approximately 10 min to obtain a homogenous mixture. During manual grinding, complexation occurs between inorganic zinc and organic carbon-based molecules, setting the stage for the subsequent synthesis of C-ZnO nanoparticles. Upon heating the resultant mixture in a quartz tube furnace at approximately 500 °C under a nitrogen atmosphere, the thermal degradation of furfural uniformly distributes carbon within the zinc oxide matrix. Remarkably, furfural fulfills a dual purpose in this synthetic route: it acts as a carbon source for doping, enhancing the photocatalytic efficacy of ZnO, and concurrently impeding the agglomeration of the nanoparticles, thus yielding a uniform nanostructured material. Adjusting the furfural volume (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, and 1.0 mL) allowed the fine-tuning of the carbon levels in ZnO, denoted as C-Z-1 to C-Z-5, respectively. This gradation of carbon content is instrumental in systematically exploring its influence on the photocatalytic activity of the material. For benchmarking purposes, a pristine ZnO reference sample (ZnO-0) was synthesized under identical conditions but without furfural. The innovation of this methodology lies in its minimalism and eco-friendliness, potentially revolutionizing the production of carbon-doped nanostructures by providing an accessible, low-cost, and scalable alternative to traditional nanoparticle-doping techniques. This has significant implications for sustainable material development, particularly for applications in environmental remediation and solar-energy harnessing.

Introduction The efficiency of zinc oxide (ZnO) nanoparticles for environmental decontamination is limited by their reliance on ultraviolet (UV) light and rapid charge carrier recombination. Carbon doping has been proposed to address these challenges by potentially enhancing visible light absorption and charge separation.

Objectives This study aims to introduce a novel, single-step synthesis method for carbon-doped ZnO (C-Z) nanoparticles, leveraging the decomposition of zinc nitrate hexahydrate and furfural under a nitrogen atmosphere to improve photocatalytic activity under visible light.

Methods A series of C-Z variants (C-Z-1 to C-Z-5) and an undoped sample (ZnO-0) were synthesized. The influence of furfural on the synthesis process and doping mechanism was analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and UV–visible diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS).

Results XPS confirmed the integration of carbon within the ZnO matrix, and XRD indicated increased lattice dimensions owing to doping. DRS revealed bandgap narrowing, suggesting enhanced charge separation. Among the variants, C-Z-3 significantly outperformed the others, showing a 12-fold increase in the photocatalytic degradation rate of Rhodamine B compared to undoped ZnO.

Conclusion The developed single-step synthesis method for C-Z nanoparticles represents a major advancement in materials engineering for ecological applications. The enhanced photocatalytic activity under visible light, as demonstrated by C-Z-3, underscores the potential of these nanoparticles for environmental decontamination.

Introduction Burgeoning concerns over environmental sustainability and energy conservation have raised the issue of escalating water pollution to the limelight  [1] ,  [2] ,  [3] . The insidious infiltration of water systems by organic pollutants, which exhibit formidable resistance to degradation under environmental stress, has spurred a scientific quest for solutions. Among these pollutants, synthetic organic dyes are recognized as the principal agents for the deterioration of water quality and disruption of aquatic life  [3] ,  [4] ,  [5] . In response to this pressing issue, the scientific community has dedicated extensive research to devise effective and economical strategies for pollution abatement. Strategies include adsorption, advanced heterogeneous photocatalysis, flocculation, and membrane-based redox reactions. These techniques are lauded not only for their cost efficiency, but also for their capacity to achieve complete mineralization of organic carbon compounds while operating under benign environmental conditions  [5] ,  [6] ,  [7] ,  [8] ,  [9] ,  [10] . In the arena of these techniques, semiconductor-based materials have emerged as a cornerstone in the domain of photocatalysis. This category, which encompasses titanium oxide, iron oxide, zinc oxide, and others, is leveraged for its proficiency in decontaminating water and generating hydrogen fuel catalyzed by ultraviolet and visible light irradiation. The mechanism at the heart of these materials involves harnessing photoinduced carriers, which play a pivotal role in the oxidative decomposition of pollutants, thus exemplifying the synergy between technological advancement and environmental stewardship  [10] ,  [11] ,  [12] ,  [13] . Zinc oxide (ZnO) has been identified as an exceptionally promising material for photocatalytic applications because of its advantageous properties including remarkable optical clarity, electrical conductivity, catalytic efficiency, chemical stability, and nontoxicity. Despite these benefits, the effectiveness of ZnO as a photocatalyst is hindered by its inherently wide bandgap, which limits its absorption of visible light, a significant component of the solar spectrum  [13] ,  [14] ,  [15] ,  [16] ,  [17] ,  [18] . Additionally, the rapid recombination of photoexcited charge carriers poses a substantial challenge, curtailing the efficiency of photocatalytic processes. To address these limitations and harness the full potential of ZnO in solar energy applications, extensive research has been directed towards modifying its photoresponse to visible light and improving its charge-carrier dynamics. A variety of innovative techniques have been employed, including but not limited to, surface engineering, hybridization with carbon materials, doping with various metals, and molecular modifications  [18] ,  [19] ,  [20] . These modifications aimed to boost the quantum yield and extend the lifespan of the photogenerated electrons and holes. In particular, carbonaceous materials have proven to be highly advantageous for such modifications because of their inherently high electrical conductivity and the versatility they offer in composite formations. By integrating carbon materials with ZnO, it is possible to create carbon-doped ZnO (C-Z) composites that not only display improved electronic properties but also exhibit enhanced thermal stability and corrosion  [21] ,  [22] ,  [23] ,  [24] ,  [25] . The result is a hybrid material that leverages the exceptional conductive properties of carbon while retaining the photocatalytic benefits of ZnO and ensuring that the process remains cost-effective, scalable, and amenable to existing manufacturing technologies. Such advancements have paved the way for ZnO-based photocatalysts to play a pivotal role in environmental purification and solar energy conversion applications, presenting a sustainable path for addressing some of the most pressing global environmental challenges  [25] ,  [26] ,  [27] ,  [28] . The integration of ZnO with carbon-based nanomaterials, such as structurally intricate carbon nanotubes, two-dimensional graphene, and minute carbon quantum dots, has emerged as a strategic innovation to amplify its photocatalytic efficiency. This amalgamation not only enhances the stability of ZnO against photodegradation but also increases its capacity to harness solar energy for environmental remediation processes. Several synthesis methodologies have been investigated to optimize the synergy between ZnO and carbon. A streamlined approach has gained prominence owing to its simplicity and eco-friendliness  [29] ,  [30] ,  [31] . This method leverages the self-assembly properties of oligomeric carbon precursors alongside Zn sources, which, upon undergoing controlled thermal treatment, coalesce to form C-Z composites with enhanced photocatalytic characteristics. Historical evidence from research conducted approximately eight years ago underscores the efficacy of ascorbic acid, a common vitamin C variant, as a carbon source. The C-Z composites synthesized using ascorbic acid showed a marked improvement in the absorption of visible light and degradation of pollutants, outperforming traditional pure ZnO nanostructures  [32] ,  [33] ,  [34] ,  [35] . Additionally, a facile and economically viable synthesis route was established that relied on the adsorption of a carbon source, citric acid, onto ZnO, followed by calcination. This not only embeds carbon into the ZnO matrix, improving its adsorptive qualities, but also results in a composite that exhibits a significant improvement in photocatalytic activity. This activity is crucial for breaking down organic contaminants under visible light and enhancing the practical applicability of C-Z composites in water treatment and air purification  [35] ,  [36] ,  [37] ,  [38] ,  [39] ,  [40] . Furthermore, these methods minimize the reliance on hazardous substances and the elaborate preparation steps that are common in composite material synthesis. As a result, the door has been opened to cost-effective, scalable production of C-Z composites, aligning with the industry's push towards sustainability and lower environmental impact. Ongoing development in this area indicates a bright future for ZnO-based materials in the advancement of green technology solutions  [40] ,  [41] ,  [42] ,  [43] ,  [44] ,  [45] ,  [46] ,  [47] . C-Z composites offer a transformative approach to the synthesis of photocatalytic materials using a novel surfactant-free synthetic strategy. This method significantly simplifies the process by eliminating the need for toxic chemicals and intricate procedures, using furfural as both a carbon source and a growth inhibitor for ZnO nanoparticles. This results in highly crystalline, finely divided nanoparticles embedded within the carbon matrix, enhancing their photocatalytic efficacy under visible light. The developed C-Z composites showed a remarkable ability to degrade organic pollutants, such as Rhodamine B dye, outperforming traditional ZnO nanostructures. This superior performance is likely due to the enhanced electrical conductivity, intrinsic defects, narrowed bandgap, and efficient photoinduced charge carrier separation. These properties were tuned by varying the furfural concentration to optimize the photocatalytic activity of the composites, making them safer and more environmentally friendly. This study has significant potential for industrial applications in water treatment and air purification, aligning with global sustainability goals and advancing the field of green technology  [5] ,  [6] ,  [7] ,  [8] . We present a novel surfactant-free strategy for the synthesis of highly crystalline C-Z materials featuring finely divided ZnO nanoparticles. This method is both straightforward and economical and consists of a singular chemical reaction stage followed by the thermal decomposition of varying proportions of a carbon-based precursor, furfural. Furfural serves a dual function: it acts as a carbon donor and simultaneously impedes the coalescence of ZnO particles. Notably, our method is simple and does not require intricate procedures, surfactants, or toxic substances that are commonly used in other protocols  [4] ,  [5] ,  [6] ,  [7] ,  [8] ,  [9] . We conducted a thorough examination of the synthesized C-Z materials using established analytical techniques, with a particular focus on their photocatalytic properties, which were assessed by observing the degradation rate of Rhodamine B dye when subjected to visible-light exposure. Our findings suggest that the optimal C-Z material exhibits an exceptional ability to degrade contaminants under visible light, likely owing to several factors: enhanced electrical conductivity, presence of intrinsic defects, narrowed band gap, and efficient photoinduced charge carrier separation. To contextualize these results, we also explored the impact of varying furfural concentrations on the synthesis of C-Z materials and assessed their photocatalytic activities in comparison with their unmodified counterparts.

Materials and method Materials The requisite chemicals for the synthesis and analysis processes, namely furfural, zinc nitrate hexahydrate, rhodamine B, benzoquinone, isopropyl alcohol, and sodium bicarbonate, were sourced from Sigma-Aldrich. These reagents were utilized directly as supplied without further purification or modification, ensuring that the experimental conditions remained consistent and that the results were reproducible and reliable based on the standardized quality of these materials. Simplified synthesis of C-Z nanostructures The fabrication of C-Z nanostructures is a pioneering and simplified method that does not require surfactants, pH adjustment, centrifugation, or hazardous chemicals. This novel approach demands only two precursor substances: zinc nitrate hexahydrate (Zn(NO 3 ) 2 ·6H 2 O) and the organic compound furfural (C 4 H 3 OCHO). The procedure began by manually blending the precursors in a mortar using a pestle for approximately 10 min to obtain a homogenous mixture. During manual grinding, complexation occurs between inorganic zinc and organic carbon-based molecules, setting the stage for the subsequent synthesis of C-ZnO nanoparticles. Upon heating the resultant mixture in a quartz tube furnace at approximately 500 °C under a nitrogen atmosphere, the thermal degradation of furfural uniformly distributes carbon within the zinc oxide matrix. Remarkably, furfural fulfills a dual purpose in this synthetic route: it acts as a carbon source for doping, enhancing the photocatalytic efficacy of ZnO, and concurrently impeding the agglomeration of the nanoparticles, thus yielding a uniform nanostructured material. Adjusting the furfural volume (0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, and 1.0 mL) allowed the fine-tuning of the carbon levels in ZnO, denoted as C-Z-1 to C-Z-5, respectively. This gradation of carbon content is instrumental in systematically exploring its influence on the photocatalytic activity of the material. For benchmarking purposes, a pristine ZnO reference sample (ZnO-0) was synthesized under identical conditions but without furfural. The innovation of this methodology lies in its minimalism and eco-friendliness, potentially revolutionizing the production of carbon-doped nanostructures by providing an accessible, low-cost, and scalable alternative to traditional nanoparticle-doping techniques. This has significant implications for sustainable material development, particularly for applications in environmental remediation and solar-energy harnessing. Characterization The detailed structural composition and crystalline phases of the C-Z were meticulously characterized through advanced X-ray diffraction (XRD) using a state-of-the-art PANalytical X’pert PRO-MPD diffractometer, originating from the Netherlands, featuring the use of copper Kα radiation characterized by a wavelength of 0.15405 nm. This technique allowed the precise determination of the crystallinity of the nanocomposites. The surface topography and microstructural characteristics of C-Z were examined using advanced scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with a HITACHI-S4800 model and high-resolution field emission transmission electron microscopy (FE-TEM) using a Tecnai G2 F20 from FEI, USA. This high-voltage (200 kV) FE-TEM not only provides detailed images of the nanocomposites, but also includes an energy filter that enables elemental mapping, which is crucial for understanding the distribution of carbon within the ZnO matrix. The TEM capabilities were further expanded to include selected-area electron diffraction patterns, allowing for the identification of crystal orientations and phase structures, as well as energy-dispersive spectrometry for quantitative chemical analysis. In the case of a specially selected sample, its morphology and internal structure were examined via SEM using a HITACHI-S4200, which provided complementary insights to those gathered by FE-TEM. The chemical states and nature of the bonds present within the nanocomposites were probed with high precision using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) on an ESCALAB 250 instrument. The XPS employed monochromatic Al Kα X-rays, with a photon energy of 1486.6 eV, to deeply analyze the electronic environment of the constituent atoms. A custom-assembled visible light source from 3 M USA was used for the experimental verification of the photocatalytic and photoelectrochemical activities. This specialized light source was tailored to deliver a specific intensity of 31 mW/cm 2  at a targeted wavelength of 450 nm, which is particularly suitable for the activation of photocatalytic processes within the C-Z nanocomposites. This light source setup is integral to simulating real-world light conditions for assessing the performance of materials in applications such as water purification and solar energy conversion. Assessment of visible Light-Induced photocatalytic degradation To assess the photocatalytic capabilities of the prepared samples, a standard procedure that focused on the degradation of Rhodamine B (RhB) under visible light was employed. The protocol commenced with a dispersion of 250 mg/L of the catalyst in an aqueous solution of RhB. This mixture was subjected to sonication to ensure a homogenous distribution of the catalyst within the solution. Subsequently, the suspension was magnetically stirred for 30 min, which was deemed sufficient to establish an equilibrium between the dye and catalyst, optimizing the adsorption–desorption dynamics. Upon reaching equilibrium, the solution was irradiated with visible light. At predetermined intervals during the irradiation process, 2 mL samples were extracted from the suspension. These samples were then centrifuged to separate the catalyst particles, yielding a clear supernatant for the analysis of photocatalytic degradation efficiency.

Results and discussion Proposed mechanism The evolution of nanoparticle synthesis has marked a shift towards more sustainable and cost-effective methodologies, as demonstrated by recent strides in non-aqueous and non-hydrolytic processes. This novel approach emphasizes the synthesis of composites (C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5), bypassing the conventional reliance on aqueous systems, surfactants, and solvents ( Fig. 1 ). This study elucidates a pioneering method that employs zinc nitrate hexahydrate and furfural to form a zinc-furfural complex. This complex was subjected to a simplified thermal treatment, ultimately yielding self-supporting C-ZnO frameworks (C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5). This methodology eschews the inclusion of water, averting the hydrolytic reactions typical of traditional routes and advancing a more streamlined and eco-friendly synthesis. Innovative synthesis proceeds sequentially. The initial stage involved a nitrate group exchange with an aldehyde group, resulting in the formation of a zinc aldehyde by expelling the hexahydrate moiety. The second stage involves the carbonization of furfural, which leads to the infusion of carbon into the ZnO lattice. The resulting reddish-brown product is a telltale sign of ligand exchange reactions, which are known to proceed even at ambient temperatures and are further facilitated by drying the complex in an environment devoid of moisture  [11] ,  [12] ,  [13] ,  [14] ,  [15] ,  [16] ,  [17] ,  [18] . The simplicity of this method is further underscored by the absence of visible changes when furfural or zinc nitrate were used alone, signifying the importance of their combination for synthesis. Thermal treatment in an inert nitrogen atmosphere is a pivotal step for producing a solid, ash-like, and remarkably lightweight product in high yield. This treatment induces a series of chemical reactions, including intermolecular cross-linking and dehydration of furfural, revealing the intricate chemistry of the furfural molecule, which contains both an aldehyde group and a conjugated system. The furfural not only undergoes carbonization but also engages in a diverse array of reactions, such as acylation, aldol condensation, and decarboxylation. The formation of C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5 was attributed to the initial ligand exchange, forming a zinc aldehyde, and subsequently producing nanosized zinc oxide or hydroxide. The furan produced from furfural can then crosslink and bond with ZnO to form a Zn-O-C-O-Zn network. As thermal decomposition progresses, carbonization of furan occurs. Furan oligomers may either evolve into diafuryl compounds or decompose into carbon monoxide and gaseous hydrocarbons. Thus, the functional groups are carbonized and robustly affixed to the ZnO particle surface, leading to the nucleation and growth of an extensive Zn-O-Zn network. This innovative synthetic pathway presents a paradigm shift in nanoparticle production, prioritizing solvent-, surfactant-, and water-free processes, thereby simplifying the investigation of potential chemical reaction pathways and minimizing environmental impacts. Moreover, the inherent simplicity of the process and the avoidance of complex reagents or additional substances render it economically favorable  [15] ,  [16] ,  [17] ,  [18] . In the broader context of materials science, such advancements in nanoparticle synthesis hold promise for revolutionizing industry standards, offering a more efficient and environmentally friendly route to material fabrication. This study not only provides a blueprint for the synthesis of C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5, but also paves the way for future exploration of similar methodologies for other composite materials. The implications of this research are vast and extend to various applications in electronics, catalysis, and environmental remediation, where the unique properties of nanoparticles are leveraged  [20] ,  [21] ,  [22] ,  [23] . The findings of this study contribute to the growing body of work seeking to align nanoparticle synthesis with the principles of green chemistry. By eliminating the need for surfactants and solvents, this study presents a leap forward in reducing the chemical footprint of nanoparticle synthesis. The adaptability of the process to ambient conditions and avoidance of complex procedures underscore its potential for scalability and industrial application  [23] ,  [24] ,  [25] ,  [26] ,  [27] ,  [28] . The surfactant-free, nonaqueous synthesis of C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5 represents a significant advancement in the field of nanotechnology, offering a synthetic route that is both environmentally benign and economically viable. The process described in this study exemplifies the potential for innovation in materials science, where efficiency, sustainability, and simplicity are at the forefront of R&D. As the field continues to evolve, such methodologies will play a critical role in shaping the future of nanoparticle synthesis and its applications. Structural, morphological, and compositional analysis The structural integrity and phase purity of ZnO-0 are of paramount importance for tailoring its properties for advanced applications. In this context, X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis is critical for elucidating the effects of carbon doping on ZnO. Our XRD investigations reveal that both the undoped baseline (ZnO-0) and the carbon-doped (C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5) samples retain the hallmark hexagonal wurtzite structure with peak position of the 2θ of 31.82°, 34.40°, 36.20°, 47.53°, 56.58°, 62.95°, 66.41°, 68.01°, 69.18°, 72.53°, and 76.91°, consistent with JCPDS card number 36–1451 ( Fig. 2 a-c). This finding highlights the ability of the doping process to integrate carbon without altering the fundamental crystal structure of ZnO. The absence of discrete carbon-related peaks within the 20-30° 2θ range in the C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5 could suggest the incorporation of carbon in an amorphous form or at concentrations that fall below the detection limit of XRD. This notion is supported by the increased noise levels observed in the XRD patterns of ZnO-0, C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5, which mirror the findings of other research and suggests the presence of carbon in noncrystalline phases  [15] ,  [16] ,  [17] ,  [18] . Moreover, the peak broadening in C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5, when juxtaposed with ZnO-0, signifies a reduction in the crystallite size, according to the Scherrer equation. This is indicative of the disruption of the ZnO lattice by carbon atoms, leading to a denser and more disordered structure ( Fig. 2 c). Such an effect has been noted in similar systems studied by Zhang et al.  [17] , in which carbon doping was found to be a significant factor contributing to the broadening of the XRD peak owing to the introduction of lattice strain. Additionally, a noteworthy peak shift towards lower angles in the carbon-doped sample indicated the interstitial incorporation of carbon or the formation of carbon-related defects. This doping-induced lattice expansion is consistent with the generation of residual stress within the ZnO matrix, affirming the interplay between dopant concentration and lattice distortion. Intriguingly, the synthesis of ZnO via thermal degradation of the zinc nitrate complex showed that ZnO prepared without furfural exhibited the highest crystallinity, a testimony to the role of the organic ligand in determining the quality of the resultant nanoparticles  [12] ,  [13] ,  [14] ,  [15] ,  [16] . These synthesized nanoparticles, devoid of Zn(NO 3 ) 2  and ZnO impurities, confirmed the efficacy of the synthetic route in yielding high-purity ZnO, which could be essential for specific electronic and optoelectronic applications. This confirms that carbon doping introduces notable variations in the XRD patterns of ZnO, as reflected in peak broadening and shifting, suggesting induced structural changes. These findings are instrumental in understanding the consequent alterations in the electronic and mechanical properties, offering valuable insights for the strategic design of C-Z in various technological arenas. The structural properties of the synthesized ZnO-0 and C-Z-4 were investigated using digital camera imaging and SEM analysis. The digital images highlight the defects or unadorned state of ZnO as a result of the direct thermal processing of the zinc nitrate-furfural combination. Proposed mechanism The evolution of nanoparticle synthesis has marked a shift towards more sustainable and cost-effective methodologies, as demonstrated by recent strides in non-aqueous and non-hydrolytic processes. This novel approach emphasizes the synthesis of composites (C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5), bypassing the conventional reliance on aqueous systems, surfactants, and solvents ( Fig. 1 ). This study elucidates a pioneering method that employs zinc nitrate hexahydrate and furfural to form a zinc-furfural complex. This complex was subjected to a simplified thermal treatment, ultimately yielding self-supporting C-ZnO frameworks (C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5). This methodology eschews the inclusion of water, averting the hydrolytic reactions typical of traditional routes and advancing a more streamlined and eco-friendly synthesis. Innovative synthesis proceeds sequentially. The initial stage involved a nitrate group exchange with an aldehyde group, resulting in the formation of a zinc aldehyde by expelling the hexahydrate moiety. The second stage involves the carbonization of furfural, which leads to the infusion of carbon into the ZnO lattice. The resulting reddish-brown product is a telltale sign of ligand exchange reactions, which are known to proceed even at ambient temperatures and are further facilitated by drying the complex in an environment devoid of moisture  [11] ,  [12] ,  [13] ,  [14] ,  [15] ,  [16] ,  [17] ,  [18] . The simplicity of this method is further underscored by the absence of visible changes when furfural or zinc nitrate were used alone, signifying the importance of their combination for synthesis. Thermal treatment in an inert nitrogen atmosphere is a pivotal step for producing a solid, ash-like, and remarkably lightweight product in high yield. This treatment induces a series of chemical reactions, including intermolecular cross-linking and dehydration of furfural, revealing the intricate chemistry of the furfural molecule, which contains both an aldehyde group and a conjugated system. The furfural not only undergoes carbonization but also engages in a diverse array of reactions, such as acylation, aldol condensation, and decarboxylation. The formation of C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5 was attributed to the initial ligand exchange, forming a zinc aldehyde, and subsequently producing nanosized zinc oxide or hydroxide. The furan produced from furfural can then crosslink and bond with ZnO to form a Zn-O-C-O-Zn network. As thermal decomposition progresses, carbonization of furan occurs. Furan oligomers may either evolve into diafuryl compounds or decompose into carbon monoxide and gaseous hydrocarbons. Thus, the functional groups are carbonized and robustly affixed to the ZnO particle surface, leading to the nucleation and growth of an extensive Zn-O-Zn network. This innovative synthetic pathway presents a paradigm shift in nanoparticle production, prioritizing solvent-, surfactant-, and water-free processes, thereby simplifying the investigation of potential chemical reaction pathways and minimizing environmental impacts. Moreover, the inherent simplicity of the process and the avoidance of complex reagents or additional substances render it economically favorable  [15] ,  [16] ,  [17] ,  [18] . The implications of this research are vast and extend to various applications in electronics, catalysis, and environmental remediation, where the unique properties of nanoparticles are leveraged  [20] ,  [21] ,  [22] ,  [23] . Catalytic actions under visible light and their underlying mechanisms To study the degradation efficiency of the commonly used industrial dye, Rhodamine B (RhB), researchers have focused on the impact of carbon additives on zinc oxide (ZnO) photocatalysts under both light and dark conditions. The experiments were carefully designed to isolate the effects of illumination from the catalytic process. It was found that ZnO without carbon doping, referred to as ZnO-0, was largely ineffective under dark conditions and visible light because of its wide band gap and the rapid recombination of its charge carriers ( Fig. 7 a-d). Conversely, the C-doped ZnO variants labeled C-Z-1 through C-Z-5 demonstrated varying degrees of improved activity when exposed to visible light. Notably, the C-Z-4 variant showed a remarkable increase in photocatalytic performance, likely owing to its narrow bandgap, which allowed for more efficient light absorption and charge carrier generation. In contrast, the C-Z catalysts, denoted as C-Z-1 through C-Z-5, presented a different picture under visible light exposure. Notably, C-Z-4 was the most efficient, with a rate constant of 0.02028/min. This value is particularly striking when compared to that of undoped ZnO-0, as it is almost 15 times higher, signifying a substantial increase in the photocatalytic degradation efficiency. The other catalysts, C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, and C-Z-5, showed rate constants of 0.00304, 0.00349, 0.01619, and 0.01282/min, respectively, indicating enhanced activity, which was not as pronounced as that of C-Z-4 ( Fig. 7 a &b). The undoped ZnO catalyst, referred to as ZnO-0, revealed a rate constant of 0.00139/min, indicating negligible activity. This efficiency was quantified using the rate constants for each catalyst, with C-Z-4 displaying a rate twelvefold greater than that of undoped ZnO-0. The superior performance of C-Z-4 can also be partially attributed to the synergistic effect between carbon and ZnO, which promotes better electron-hole separation. This is crucial because effective photocatalysis is not just a matter of light absorption; the movement of electron-hole pairs to the reaction sites is equally significant. The reusability of C-Z-4 was confirmed through multiple cycles, indicating its potential for practical application in industrial settings owing to its stability and sustained activity. In recent research focusing on the photocatalytic degradation of pollutants under visible light irradiation, a comparative analysis of undoped ZnO (ZnO-0) and a series of C-Z nanostructures (C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5) revealed significant differences in their photocatalytic performances. Undoped ZnO-0 displays relatively poor photocatalytic activity for the degradation of Rhodamine B (RhB), a common dye pollutant. This inefficiency is primarily attributed to the larger particle size, which limits the surface area available for effective interactions with the RhB molecules. The surface area (92.35 m 2 /g) and BJH adsorption average pore diameter (77.17 Å) observed for the optimized catalyst which are also supported the present catalysts performance. In contrast, the C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5 nanostructures exhibited enhanced photocatalytic abilities under similar conditions. This improvement is multifaceted and involves several key factors. First, the doping of carbon into ZnO created vacant sites near the valence band, effectively reducing the bandgap energy ( Fig. 7 c). This reduction in the bandgap allows these doped nanostructures to absorb more light energy from the visible spectrum, which is crucial for initiating the photocatalytic process. Additionally, the presence of impurity levels in the doped structures facilitates the generation of holes, which play a pivotal role in photocatalytic mechanisms. These holes participated in the oxidative half-cycle, converting water molecules into hydroxyl radicals (HO • ). These radicals are highly reactive and contribute significantly to RhB degradation. Moreover, under visible-light exposure, the electrons in the doped nanostructures were excited from the valence band to the conduction band. The narrow bandgaps of C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5 facilitated this transition. Once in the conduction band, these photogenerated electrons interact with the dissolved oxygen in the water, leading to the formation of superoxide radical anions ( • O 2 – ). These anions, along with hydroxyl radicals, formed potent combinations that actively participated in the breakdown of RhB molecules. This study underscores the intricate interplay between the structural and photophysical properties of the C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5 nanostructures and their impact on photocatalytic efficiency. These findings highlight the potential of these modified nanostructures for environmental applications, particularly for the degradation of organic pollutants. Thus, this research opens new avenues for developing more effective photocatalytic materials, leveraging the unique properties of nanostructured composites for environmental remediation ( Fig. 7 d).

Analyzing the superior photocatalytic efficacy of C-Z: An examination of Photo-Physical Properties, mobility Gap, and the density of states in valence and conduction bands Diffuse absorption spectra and band gap energy The diffuse absorption spectra of ZnO-0 and its carbon-doped variants, C-Z-1-C-Z-5, revealed distinct optical properties. The carbon-doped samples exhibited stronger absorption in the visible spectrum than ZnO-0, with absorption edges extending to approximately 700–750 nm, which is advantageous for solar energy capture ( Fig. 8 a & b). This redshift in the absorption edge of the doped samples suggests an interaction between carbon and ZnO, which is likely a consequence of the fabrication process. The optical assessment of these materials is critical, particularly in photocatalytic applications, where light interactions dictate their performance. Narrowing of the bandgap, which enhances the visible-light response, can be induced by carbon doping or by the creation of oxygen vacancies. Calculations based on established formulas have determined the bandgap energies of ZnO-0 and the doped samples to be 3.10 eV and progressively lower for C-Z-1 to C-Z-5, with the latter having bandgaps as low as 2.31 eV ( Fig. 8 b). This trend of a decreasing bandgap with increasing carbon content indicates that carbon incorporation effectively modified the defect landscape within the ZnO structure, thereby tuning the optical bandgap. This tunability suggests that carbon doping in ZnO can be a strategic approach for engineering materials with the desired optical properties for enhanced photocatalytic activity. Density of states in valence and conduction bands To deepen our understanding of the reduced band gap and enhanced photophysical characteristics of series C-Z-1 to C-Z-5, we examined their DOS. This analysis was based on data from UV–visible diffuse absorption and valence-band (VB) X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS). Focusing on C-Z-2 through C-Z-5, we explored the band gap narrowing using VB XPS and calculated the DOS by integrating the results from visible diffuse absorption spectroscopy ( Fig. 9 a-c). For comparison, P-TiO 2  exhibited a valence band DOS with a peak energy edge at approximately 2.20 eV, which is consistent with prior studies. In contrast, the peak energies of C-Z-2-C-Z-5 were determined to be approximately 2.85 eV. The optical bandgap energies were identified as 3.15 eV for ZnO-0 and 2.71 eV for the C-Z series. From these observations, the absorption onset in the C-Z series was pinpointed at approximately 2.85 eV, with a significant band tail at approximately 0.65 eV ( Fig. 9 b). This indicates a notable bandgap reduction in the C-Z series, likely due to a slight tailing in the valence band, which is a common feature of carbon doping. The combination of these findings with optical band gap measurements indicated a decrease in the band gap of the C-Z series. This reduction is hypothesized to stem from the displacement or substitution of carbon within the ZnO lattice, which affects the valence band maxima and facilitates the band gap reduction in ZnO-0. Photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy has been instrumental in evaluating the photophysical characteristics of ZnO and carbon-modified ZnO samples, providing insights into the dynamics of electron-hole pairs. According to the PL spectra, all samples, including ZnO-0 and C-Z-1 through C-Z-5, emitted excitonic signals with a consistent shape, indicating that the presence of carbon did not introduce additional PL emissions ( Fig. 10 a and b). Notably, the carbon-doped samples exhibited two prominent peaks, with the first at approximately 382–390 nm corresponding to bandgap emissions from free carrier recombination and the second, a broad emission at approximately 520 nm, attributed to defects within the ZnO crystal structure. Crucially, the intensity of the PL emissions in the carbon-doped samples was markedly reduced compared with that of pure ZnO-0, suggesting a lower recombination rate of photoexcited electrons and holes. This reduction indicates an enhanced separation of charge carriers, which is likely facilitated by the presence of carbon on the ZnO surface. This feature is indicative of the potential for higher photocatalytic performance in the doped samples, as a suppressed recombination rate is beneficial for photocatalytic processes. Therefore, ZnO materials modified by carbon doping are expected to exhibit superior photocatalytic activity relative to their undoped counterparts. Two significant peaks are observed in the emission spectra of ZnO-0, C-Z-1, C-Z-2, C-Z-3, C-Z-4, and C-Z-5. The first peak, which occurs at approximately 390 nm, is attributed to the near-bandgap emission (NBE) caused by the recombination of free charge carriers. The second peak, a broad deep-level (DL) emission at approximately 530 nm, often referred to as green emission, arises from the radial recombination of a photogenerated hole with a singly ionized charge state of defects within the ZnO crystal structure. Insights into the crystalline structures of the photocatalysts were obtained by analyzing the IDL/INBE ratio, which compares the intensities of the DL and NBE peaks. ZnO-0 demonstrated the highest IDL/INBE ratio, indicating a greater prevalence of defects, primarily oxygen vacancies, which is consistent with the DRS results. Conversely, the C-Z series (C-Z-1 to C-Z-5) showed a progressive decrease in this ratio with increasing inclusion of aniline, suggesting an improvement in the crystallinity of ZnO. This characterization implies that the C-Z series of photocatalysts possess a higher carbon content and more defective structure than ZnO-0.

Conclusions In conclusion, the innovative single-step synthesis of C-Z nanoparticles utilizing the unique decomposition of zinc nitrate hexahydrate and furfural under a nitrogen atmosphere, marks a significant advancement in the fields of material science and photocatalysis. This method effectively integrated carbon into the ZnO matrix, as evidenced by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, which demonstrated that carbon atoms occupied the oxygen vacancies. This doping resulted in enlarged lattice dimensions, as observed in the X-ray diffraction analyses, and a narrowed bandgap, as identified through UV–visible diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS). These modifications enhanced the charge separation capacity of the nanoparticles, making them more efficient for photocatalytic applications. The array of synthesized C-Z variants, particularly C-Z-4, exhibited remarkable photocatalytic performance. C-Z-4 significantly outperformed undoped ZnO in degrading Rhodamine B, showing a 12-fold increase in the degradation rate. This demonstrates the potential of C-Z nanoparticles, especially C-Z-4, for environmental decontamination using visible light. Such a facile and efficient synthesis strategy not only offers a promising route for producing high-performance photocatalysts, but also represents a crucial step forward in developing sustainable solutions for ecological challenges. This study underscores the importance of materials engineering in addressing environmental issues, with C-Z nanoparticles emerging as key players in green technology.
